lesson.title: Find the intended row

steps.headline: A row has a label and a position, and loc and iloc read them differently.

lead.text: Every row of a DataFrame has a label in its index and a place in the table. With labels 10, 20 and 30, the label 10 sits at position 0. loc looks rows up by label. iloc looks them up by position, counted from zero.
loc asks for a label, not a place in the list. Pair each label with its value first.

reveal.text: You read a value by its label, not by counting along. With loc, the label is what matters, wherever the row sits.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[20, 'units']

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[1, 0]

steps.headline: With labels 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25, how many rows do df.loc[10:20] and df.iloc[1:3] select?

workedSteps.text: loc slices by label and includes both ends: 10, 15 and 20.
iloc slices by position and stops before the end: positions 1 and 2.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[10:20]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[0:1]

steps.headline: With labels 10, 20, 30 and 40, how many rows do df.loc[20:40] and df.iloc[1:3] select?

workedSteps.text: loc includes both end labels: 20, 30 and 40. How many rows is that?
iloc starts at position 1 and stops before position 3. How many rows is that?

lead.text: In df.iloc[r, c], the first value picks the row position and the second picks the column position, both counted from zero. loc takes labels in the same two places.

reveal.text: You counted a row position and a column position, each from zero. The first value always picks rows and the second picks columns.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[[10, 30], ['price']]

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[[0, 2], [1]]

steps.headline: Assigning a Series to a column matches values by index label, not by order.

lead.text: When pandas stores a Series in a column, it lines up the labels first. A Series written in a different order still lands on the rows with the same labels. A plain list has no labels, so it fills the rows by position.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill']}, index=[10, 20])
df['units'] = pd.Series([8, 3], index=[20, 10])

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill']}, index=[10, 20])
df['units'] = [8, 3]

lead.text: A DataFrame has rows labelled 1 and 2. You assign pd.Series([50, 60], index=[2, 1]) as a new column.

reveal.text: The labels decided where each value went. Row 1 received the value that carried the label 1, even though it was written second.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish loc labels from iloc positions and recognise index alignment.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Three lockers numbered 10, 20 and 30 stand in a row. The caretaker counts their places from zero, starting at the left.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a row's label from its position, and pick the right one with loc and iloc.

recap.keyIdea: loc reads by label and iloc by position from zero, and a Series assigned to a column lines up by label.

blocks.text: You found that the locker at place 1 is number 20. You read 7 at label 20, and found row 1 receives 60 when a Series carries the label 1.

recap.nextHook: Next: keep only the rows that answer a question, using a Boolean mask.

questions.prompt: A Series has values 4, 7 and 9 at labels 10, 20 and 30. What is s.loc[20]?
hints: loc reads a label, not a position.
Pair each label with the value at the same place.
Find label 20 and read its value.
questions.onCorrect: 7. loc looked up the label 20, and its row holds the middle value.

misconceptions.feedback: That value is at label 30. loc uses the label 20.
That is the value at label 10, the first row.

questions.prompt: On sorted labels 10, 20, 30 and 40, how many rows does df.loc[20:40] select?
hints: Include both existing end labels.
List the labels from the first end to the second.
Count the labels you listed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The included labels are 20, 30 and 40. Label slicing includes the stop.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A label slice includes both ends, so the rows labelled 20, 30 and 40 are selected.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the end label as excluded. A label slice includes it.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame has columns units and price, rows labelled 10, 20 and 30, units 3, 6, 9 and price 5, 7, 2. What is df.iloc[2, 1]?
hints: The first number is a row position, the second a column position.
Count positions from zero: which row and which column is that?
Read the price in the third row.
questions.onCorrect: 2. Row position 2 is the third row, and column position 1 is price, so the value is its price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the units of the third row. Column position 1 is price.
That is the price of the second row. Row positions count from zero.

questions.prompt: A Series is assigned as a DataFrame column. How are its values matched to rows?
hints: Track the labels on both objects.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Series assignment aligns matching index labels, including when their order differs.

questions.onCorrect: By index label. pandas lines up the labels, including when the Series is written in a different order.

misconceptions.feedback: Order matters only for a plain list. A Series carries labels, which win.
Values play no part in matching. Labels do.

questions.prompt: How many rows does df.iloc[1:4] select from a six-row DataFrame?
hints: Use ordinary stop-exclusive slicing on positions.
The slice excludes its end position.
List the positions from 1 up to the end and count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It selects positions 1, 2 and 3; the stop is excluded.

questions.onCorrect: 3. The positions are 1, 2 and 3, because the stop of an iloc slice is excluded.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the stop position. iloc excludes it.

questions.prompt: A Series holds 11 and 22 at labels 'b' and 'a'. What value aligns to DataFrame row 'a'?
hints: Match the requested label.
The Series lists label b first, then label a.
Read the value paired with label a.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value with label a is 22, regardless of its position in the Series.

questions.onCorrect: 22. The value paired with label a goes to row a, wherever it sits in the Series.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first value shown, but its label is b.

hints: iloc[0] is a position and loc[30] is a label.
Position 0 is the first value.
Add that to the value at label 30.
questions.prompt: A Series has values 4, 7 and 9 at labels 10, 20 and 30. What is s.iloc[0] + s.loc[30]?
questions.onCorrect: 13. iloc[0] read the first place, 4, and loc[30] read the label 30, 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads loc[30] as position 30... use the value at label 30.
iloc[0] and loc[10] would be the same row, but loc[30] is a different one.

hints: Places start at 0 on the left.
Place 0 holds the first locker.
Place 1 is the next one along.
questions.prompt: What number is on the locker at place 1?
questions.onCorrect: 20. The number on a locker is its label, and its place is where it stands. pandas keeps those two ideas apart.

misconceptions.feedback: That locker is at place 0. Counting starts from zero.

hints: iloc counts positions, not labels.
questions.prompt: With row labels 100, 200 and 300, what does df.iloc[0] select?

choices.label: An error, because iloc needs a label

questions.onCorrect: The row labelled 100. iloc counts places from zero, so place 0 is the first row whatever its label is.

misconceptions.feedback: No row has the label 0 here. iloc uses position, not label.
iloc takes positions. It never asks for a label.

hints: Compare how each slice treats its end.
questions.prompt: Why do the two slices select different numbers of rows?

choices.label: loc includes its end label; iloc stops before its end position

acceptedIdeas: loc includes its end label; iloc stops before its end position
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Label slices include both ends; position slices exclude the stop.

questions.onCorrect: loc includes its end label, while iloc stops before its end position.

misconceptions.feedback: iloc counts from zero, like every position in Python.
loc starts exactly at its first label. It skips nothing.

hints: Positions start at 0.
Include position 1 and stop before the end position.
List the positions and count them.
questions.prompt: How many rows does df.iloc[1:3] select?
questions.onCorrect: 2. The positional slice has positions 1 and 2, and stops before 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the end position. A positional slice excludes it.

hints: Which label does each value carry?
The Series was written with labels 2 then 1.
Find the value that carries the label 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value with label 1 is 60, so row 1 receives it.

questions.onCorrect: 60. The label 1 decides it. The Series was written in the other order, but alignment follows labels.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first value written, but it carries the label 2.
